title: What is the difference between class-level and method-level @Transactional?

s1_definition.profdef: `@Transactional` on a class applies to ALL public methods as the default. `@Transactional` on a specific method OVERRIDES the class-level settings for that method. Common pattern: `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` on the class (default = read-only for all queries), then `@Transactional` (writable) on specific write methods. This prevents accidental writes in read methods and enables read-replica routing for all queries by default.
s1_definition.analogy: Class-level = a sign on the bank door: "All operations are read-only by default." Method-level = a sign on a specific counter: "THIS counter handles transfers (writable)." The specific counter's sign overrides the door sign.
s1_definition.oneliner: Class-level = default for all methods. Method-level overrides class-level. Common: readOnly=true on class, writable on write methods.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@Transactional` on a class applies to ALL public methods as the default. `@Transactional` on a specific method OVERRIDES the class-level settings for that method. Common pattern: `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` on the class (default = read-only for all queries), then `@Transactional` (writable) on specific write methods. This prevents accidental writes in read methods and enables read-replica routing for all queries by default.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Class-level = a sign on the bank door: "All operations are read-only by default." Method-level = a sign on a specific counter: "THIS counter handles transfers (writable)." The specific counter's sign overrides the door sign.

**One line to remember:** Class-level = default for all methods. Method-level overrides class-level. Common: readOnly=true on class, writable on write methods.

sections.s2_technical:
When `@Transactional` sits on a class, Spring treats it as the default transaction configuration for every public method of that bean. When `@Transactional` also sits on a specific method, the method-level settings win for that method only; the other methods keep the class-level defaults. Spring resolves this precedence through `AnnotationTransactionAttributeSource`, which checks the method first and falls back to the class.

The most common and useful pattern is `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` at the class level, so every query method automatically skips Hibernate dirty checking and can be routed to a read replica, with no annotation needed on each one. The few methods that actually write data get a method-level `@Transactional` that overrides back to writable, for example `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)` on `withdraw`. This is safer because a newly added read method is read-only by default, so a developer cannot accidentally forget the optimization or accidentally perform writes in a read path. A senior nuance: only public methods are proxied, so a class-level annotation does not affect private or self-invoked methods, and method-level overrides are the clean way to mark the handful of write operations in an otherwise read-only service.
sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's account service has 10 read methods and 3 write methods.** Without class-level @Transactional(readOnly=true), developers forget to add readOnly on each read method, missing dirty-checking optimization and read-replica routing. The team uses class-level readOnly as default, overriding only on write methods.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a balance inquiry for SAV2001 (a read) followed by a Rs.50,000 deposit to SAV2001 (a write), handled by a service with class-level readOnly.

**Step 1.** The inquiry calls `getAccount`, which has no method-level annotation, so it inherits the class-level `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`. The proxy begins a read-only transaction.

**Step 2.** Hibernate uses manual flush mode for this read, skipping dirty checking, and a routing DataSource can send the query to a read replica. The balance is returned with no write capability.

**Step 3.** The deposit calls `deposit`, which has a method-level `@Transactional` overriding the class default to writable. The proxy begins a writable transaction on the primary database.

**Step 4.** The method loads SAV2001, adds Rs.50,000, and saves. Because the transaction is writable, Hibernate dirty-checks and flushes the change at commit.

**Step 5.** The transaction commits and the new balance is durable. The same class served both a read-optimized path and a write path purely by inheriting versus overriding the annotation.

```
INFO  [exec-1] AccountService - getAccount (class readOnly=true) → flush MANUAL, replica route
INFO  [exec-2] AccountService - deposit (method-level override → writable) SAV2001 +50000
INFO  [exec-2] AccountService - COMMIT, new balance durable on primary
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  @Service
  @Transactional(readOnly = true)           ← CLASS-LEVEL DEFAULT
  class AccountService {

    getAccount()      → inherits readOnly=true  → Hibernate: NO dirty checking ✅
    getByType()       → inherits readOnly=true  → DataSource: route to READ REPLICA ✅
    getHighBalance()  → inherits readOnly=true  → fast, no flush on commit ✅
    countActive()     → inherits readOnly=true  → ✅

    @Transactional                              ← METHOD-LEVEL OVERRIDE (readOnly=false)
    deposit()         → writable TX             → dirty checking ON, writes allowed ✅

    @Transactional(rollbackFor=Exception.class) ← METHOD-LEVEL OVERRIDE
    withdraw()        → writable + rollback on checked exceptions ✅
  }

  ═══ PRECEDENCE RULE ═══
  Method-level @Transactional OVERRIDES class-level for THAT method only.
  Other methods still use class-level settings.

  ═══ BENEFIT ═══
  10 read methods: automatically readOnly (no annotation per method)
  3 write methods: explicitly writable (override class-level)
  Forgot to annotate a new read method? → readOnly by default (safe!) ✅
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Class-level Transactional applies as the default for all public methods in the service. Method-level Transactional overrides the class-level settings for that specific method. The best practice is to set Transactional readOnly equals true at the class level because most service methods are read operations. Then override with a writable Transactional on the few methods that modify data. This ensures that all read methods automatically skip Hibernate dirty checking, can be routed to a read replica by a routing DataSource, and do not accidentally perform writes. If a developer adds a new read method and forgets to annotate it, it is safe by default because the class-level readOnly applies.

In my account inquiry service, the class-level readOnly equals true covers four read methods (getAccount, getByType, getHighBalance, countActive) with zero annotations on each. The deposit and withdraw methods have method-level Transactional that overrides to writable. The withdraw method additionally specifies rollbackFor equals Exception.class to handle checked exceptions. This pattern keeps the code clean and eliminates the risk of forgetting readOnly on individual methods.
